items.title: Pondus: an agentic structural analysis and design program
items.abstract: Language-model agents can now operate engineering programs through tool interfaces, but a structuralprogram that an agent drives has to be designed for that user, because the agent accepts whatever numbersthe tools return. This paper describes Pondus, an open-source native program in which a language-modelagent and an engineer work on one three-dimensional structural model, and reports how it is built, howit is used and how far its results can be trusted. The agent reaches the program through a Model ContextProtocol server of 44 tools, either from the chat panel of the desktop application, where a vendored agentharness runs one agent session per message on a copy of the model, or from external agents such asClaude Desktop and ChatGPT. Every tool calls the same functions as the engineer’s interface, so a modelbuilt by the agent can be checked, edited and undone by hand. The analysis runs on the Stabileo engine,which Pondus links as a library with four marked changes: Pondus splits members, transfers slab loads,generates shear walls as wide columns with rigid arms and builds the seismic mass before handing asolver input to the engine, and it designs to ACI 318-19, AISC 360-16 and EN 1993-1-1 from the results.Two agent runs with a low-cost model built, analysed and designed a two-storey frame in 105 s with 13tool calls and a five-storey frame with shear walls under an ASCE 7-22 response spectrum, including a16-page calculation report, in 382 s with 22 tool calls. Every number in the agent’s answers matched thetools and hand checks of the loads, the seismic weight and the base shear, but the answers also containedfour descriptive errors, such as reporting two deepened beams where the program had deepened six, andthey did not point out that the walls resist load only in one direction, so the response modification factorof the walls was applied to the frame direction as well. A calibration against 470 published, closed-formand independent reference values over 229 cases found 430 within 0.5 % and 449 within 1 %, and itfound fourteen defects, thirteen of them in the code that prepares the inputs of the engine and the designchecks rather than in the numerical kernels. A second calibration against the verification problems thatCSI publishes for SAP2000 and ETABS reproduced 177 of 199 independent values within 0.5 % andfound eight further defects, including an unconservative omission of the Eurocode 3 moment reductionfor high shear, which led to lumped masses, the SRSS combination and frame shear deformation beingadded. Together these results suggest that the tools of an agentic structural program can be made accurate,whereas the agent’s prose remains the weaker link that the engineer must read against the program’s own tables.

items.title: “I Don’t Trust It, but I Have to Trust It”: Trust vs. Use of Online Technology Across the Mental Health Spectrum in the UK
items.abstract: Use of internet-based technologies (IBTs) and artificial intelligence (AI) via eHealth could enhance mental healthcare delivery and accessibility. However, ethical concerns, perceptions of AI capabilities, past experience, and individual differences can influence acceptance and engagement. We qualitatively explored attitudes and behaviours toward IBTs, AI and eHealth, given the overlapping nature of these digital environments, trust, and the possible role of mental health. This exploratory study conducted semi-structured interviews between March and October 2023 with 22 UK-based participants: eight with lived experience of a mental health problem and 14 without. There was no clear difference in participants’ levels of trust in IBTs across mental health status. Participants reported using IBTs despite privacy concerns. Trust was influenced by perceptions of developer trustworthiness, individual traits, and affective responses to IBTs. Convenience, ease of use, and lack of alternatives often outweighed concerns, driving engagement. Our findings highlight that in this group trust is a key factor in IBT and eHealth uptake, but not the sole determinant, highlighting ethical concerns and responsibilities for both UK healthcare providers and developers. There is a need for transparent, ethically grounded, value-sensitive design and implementation of IBTs and AI-enabled eHealth tools that supports genuine user choice, voluntary engagement, and human interaction.

items.title: A Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Learning Assessment Framework (HCAI-LAF) for Open and Distance Education
items.abstract: This chapter presents the Human Centered Artificial Intelligence Learning Assessment Framework, a conceptual model designed to support valid, equitable, and trustworthy assessment in AI enhanced Open Distance e Learning environments. The chapter addresses challenges created by generative artificial intelligence in higher education, where submitted work may not fully represent learner understanding or skill. It integrates learner engagement, artifact authenticity, AI assessment support, instructor oversight, and transparency and trust into a unified sociotechnical framework centered on Learning Evidence Validity. The framework explains how human agency, ethical oversight, and artificial intelligence tools interact to influence the quality, reliability, and fairness of assessment outcomes. The chapter further outlines construct relationships and demonstrates how the framework can guide empirical research and practical implementation across online and hybrid contexts.

items.title: A hybrid artificial intelligence framework for three-dimensional electromagnetic field mapping using airborne measurements in general aviation
items.abstract: The increasing electrification of aircraft systems and development of autonomous aviation technologies increase the need for accurate characterization of electromagnetic field (EMF) distributions under operational conditions. However, dense three-dimensional EMF measurements in aviation environments are difficult to obtain because airborne observations are typically sparse, irregularly distributed, and collected under varying flight conditions. Here, we present an artificial intelligence-based framework for three-dimensional reconstruction of the electric field component of EMF from real-world airborne measurements in general aviation. The study uses more than 80 h of measurements collected during operational activities involving four aircraft types and a low-cost, high-sensitivity sensing platform recording synchronized electric-field and geospatial data over the 1-8000 MHz frequency range. Geostatistical and machine-learning approaches, including Kriging, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, and Exact Gaussian Processes, were evaluated for three-dimensional field reconstruction. Based on this comparison, we developed a hybrid Deep Gaussian Process Kolmogorov-Arnold Feature Extractor (DGKAN), combining nonlinear feature representation with probabilistic spatial modeling and uncertainty estimation. DGKAN achieved the highest predictive accuracy, with a mean absolute error of 0.0381 and a mean squared error of 0.0071, reducing the mean absolute error by approximately 27.6% relative to the strongest baseline model. These results demonstrate that combining Kolmogorov-Arnold representations with probabilistic Gaussian Process modeling enables accurate reconstruction of three-dimensional electromagnetic field distributions from sparse airborne measurements. The proposed framework provides a data-driven approach for electromagnetic environment assessment in general aviation and establishes a basis for further development of intelligent EMF monitoring and prediction methods under operational flight conditions.

items.title: A multi-prompt transfer learning framework based on segment anything model 2 for segmenting microcracks in engineered cementitious composite images and videos
items.abstract: Accurate segmentation of engineered cementitious composites (ECC) microcracks is important for evaluating material damage and cracking behavior. However, ECC cracks are typically slender, low-contrast, and densely distributed, and can easily be confused with pores, shadows, and surface textures. Existing crack segmentation methods rely heavily on large-scale pixel-level annotations and often exhibit limited robustness when applied to ECC microcracks. To address these issues, this study proposes a multi-prompt transfer learning framework based on Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2). The framework integrates a threshold-based coarse-mask prior, a self-perceptive prompt box, and Euclidean distance transform-guided positive and negative point prompts to enhance crack localization while suppressing noise and preserving crack connectivity. In addition, a progressive unfreezing-based few-shot transfer strategy and a hybrid loss function are employed to effectively adapt the foundation model to the ECC crack domain while reducing annotation costs. Experimental results on a laboratory ECC dataset show that the proposed framework achieves a mean accuracy of 99.1%, a mean intersection over union (IoU) of 86.4%, and a Dice coefficient of 92.6%, outperforming mainstream deep learning baselines. Notably, with only five annotated training images, the framework still achieves a mean IoU of 81.7% and a Dice coefficient of 89.7%, demonstrating strong performance under a highly limited annotation budget. Without any video-specific training, the framework also achieves temporally consistent crack video segmentation through the streaming memory mechanism of SAM2. Overall, the proposed framework provides an effective and annotation-efficient method for detecting microcracks in both static images and dynamic videos.

items.title: A Multi-Stakeholder Survey Examining Incident Review Processes in a National Healthcare System: A Study Protocol
items.abstract: Background Incident reporting is central to patient safety, yet translating review findings into systemic learning remains challenging. Within the Irish Health Service Executive (HSE) 2020 Incident Management Framework (IMF), Improvement Planning and Monitoring (Step 6) is where findings are intended to become service change. How well reviews achieve this, and how the review methodologies in use shape that performance, has not been systematically examined. This protocol sets out a study examining how these methodologies operate in practice and the perceived quality of the recommendations they produce, by capturing the accounts of multiple stakeholders linked to the same reviews, with particular attention to human factors in the transition from learning to action. Methods The study uses a cross-sectional, mixed-methods survey design. A stratified random sample of 96 incident reviews will be drawn from the National Incident Management System (NIMS): 48 Category 1 (major/severe harm) and 48 Category 2 (moderate harm), equally divided between acute and community settings. Seven role-tailored instruments, mapped to four stakeholder categories (reviewers and commissioners; clinical staff; implementers; patients, service users and families), combine rating-scale and written-response questions organised around the six IMF principles. Quantitative data will be analysed using descriptive and non-parametric methods, qualitative data using reflexive thematic analysis, and the two strands integrated through joint displays. Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval has been granted by the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee at Trinity College Dublin and the HSE National Research Ethics Committee. A pilot phase of five reviews will precede national administration. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication, conference presentation, and a summary report to the HSE, and are intended to identify systemic barriers to improvement planning and inform a national logic model for shared learning.

items.title: A paradigm shift toward explainable and federated intelligence for brain tumor MRI analysis
items.abstract: Deep learning techniques in brain tumor analysis using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans have improved significantly, but their clinical deployment is limited by models with limited interpretability (‘black-box' models) and data privacy limitations. This paper analyses recent literature and aims to explore the intersection of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and Federated Learning (FL). Following the PRISMA protocol, a systematic search was conducted in Scopus on February 24, 2026, covering English-language journal articles and conference proceedings published from January 2020 to February 2026. The search initially identified 767 records, which were screened using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria for MRI-based brain tumor studies addressing deep learning, explainability, privacy, or Federated Learning, resulting in 147 initially retained studies for the final screening set. One study was subsequently identified as formally retracted and excluded from the final synthesis, resulting in 146 included studies. The review classifies the literature into five primary research themes in brain tumor analysis: explainability, deep learning frameworks, privacy-preserving learning, advanced architectures (Transformers and Mamba), and multimodal learning. The literature suggests a paradigm shift in brain tumor analysis toward model interpretability using XAI. However, there is a significant knowledge gap in privacy-preserving collaborative learning models. Advanced architectures are proposed to solve brain tumor problems, but there are still limitations in model generalization, computational costs, and clinical reliability.

items.title: A Prescriptive Design Framework for CRM-Integrated Agentic AI in Hospital Patient Services: Design Science Development and Empirical Proof-of-Concept Evaluation
items.abstract: Hospital patient services (registration and appointment scheduling) often face fragmented systems, long handling times, and data-entry errors, while patients expect instant 24/7 digital interactions. This study uses Design Science Research to develop a prescriptive five-phase framework for CRM-integrated agentic AI, whose novelty lies in combining bounded transactional agency, middleware-mediated access to CRM/SIMRS tools, and staged governance. Its design assumptions are evaluated through a controlled proof of concept (PoC). The PoC implements an end-to-end transactional conversational workflow (WhatsApp/web chat) in which an LLM-based agent uses API middleware to call tools on a CRM/SIMRS sandbox, avoiding direct database access. The artefact structures are: preparation and alignment; analysis and detailed design; implementation and controlled testing; pilot and evaluation; and scaling and institutionalization, supported by governance mechanisms (clinical “green/red” boundaries, audit logging, and human-in-the-loop supervision). Empirical evaluation applied black-box testing across 15 positive and negative scenarios comprising 285 executions. Of these, 246 met the predefined scenario criteria, and 39 failed, yielding an overall controlled-scenario success rate of 86.32%. A separate message-level latency log contained 292 message-response pairs across 58 recorded conversation groups; median response time was 9 s (IQR 4–19 s), with 88.70% of responses returned in under 30 s and 97.26% in under 60 s. Selected persisted CRM records were additionally checked through authorized visual inspection, with no discrepancies observed. These findings support technical feasibility under controlled PoC conditions while identifying patient-centred evaluation, cybersecurity assessment, production load testing, economic evaluation, longitudinal monitoring, and multi-site validation as requirements for broader deployment.

items.title: A psychological prediction automatic reasoning framework for explaining potential cognitive states
items.abstract: Psychological prediction, the ability to infer human behavior and intentions, is essential for artificial intelligence and human–machine interaction. Existing deep learning models often rely on surface-level fitting and lack structured abductive interpretability, while traditional neuro-symbolic systems suffer from non-differentiable discontinuities and limited adaptability to dynamic contextual constraints. This paper proposes a neuro-symbolic automated reasoning framework for modeling latent cognitive states under contextual constraints. The framework introduces a context-aware adaptive SMC resampling operator (CAR-SMC), which uses energy-based penalties to filter hypotheses violating contextual constraints. We further design an executable differentiable program synthesis (EDPS) module and a hybrid iterative program–cognition interaction (HIPCI) mechanism. Through stop-gradient-based directional optimization, HIPCI separates the update pathways of belief and program representations during alternating fixed-point optimization, reducing circular gradient entanglement. Experiments on OpenToM and FANToM show that the framework improves the abductive consistency rate (ACR), an empirical belief–action consistency metric, to 70.8% and 52.1%, respectively. Under the adopted classification-oriented evaluation setup, these results indicate additional ACR gains over pure fine-tuned encoder classifiers and higher ACR than the evaluated few-shot ToT reference baseline (~ 7B), while using fewer parameters and maintaining an average inference latency of 215 ms per instance. Overall, this work provides a differentiable framework for machine Theory of Mind with process-level structural interpretability under the evaluated text-based classification setting.

items.title: A Right to Delegate to AI: The Regulatory Safety Halo and the Acceleration of Agentic Consumer Markets
items.abstract: Abstract The European Law Institute’s Guiding Principles and Model Rules on Digital Assistants for Consumer Contracts (DACC) propose a right for consumers to use digital assistants in business-to-consumer relations. The DACC’s definition encompasses consumer AI agents (CAIAs), which use AI-generated outputs to determine transactionally relevant matters left open by consumers and initiate or perform transactional actions. The article examines two concerns. First, recognition and safeguards may create a regulatory safety halo, causing consumers to overestimate CAIAs’ technical reliability and the effectiveness of remedies for unwanted outcomes. Second, recognition may accelerate agentic markets, disproportionately benefit incumbents in adjacent digital markets, and foster concentration, to which the DMA and EU competition law provide only partial responses. Legislation should therefore first establish essential rules governing delegation, responsibility and market contestability. Technical implementation may be entrusted to European standardisation bodies, but the Commission’s request should define tasks precisely and maximise transparency and balanced stakeholder participation to mitigate legitimacy concerns. Only once CAIAs are sufficiently reliable and the legal framework more mature should the right to use a CAIA be recognised.

items.title: A sparse autoencoder and explainable machine learning framework for provenance tracing of historic blue bricks in architectural conservation
items.abstract: Provenance identification of historic blue bricks supports material authenticity in architectural conservation, but missing inscriptions and incomplete archives limit conventional approaches. We integrate sparse autoencoders, machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence to classify brick provenance using X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy and X-ray fluorescence data. Spectral latent features are fused with elemental concentrations, and synthetic minority oversampling addresses class imbalance. In a dataset of 52 bricks from five regions, the random forest classifier achieved 95% test accuracy and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.973. Shapley additive explanations identified Rb, Al and Zr as important discriminative variables, while decoder-based analysis linked latent features to mineral phases. Ablation and feature-substitution analyses indicated complementary elemental and spectral information. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework offers a high-accuracy and theoretically interpretable engineering solution for the provenance identification of historic blue bricks.

items.title: A systematic literature review of generative AI support for pre-service teachers in designing computational thinking instruction
items.abstract: Abstract Computational Thinking (CT) is increasingly expected across curricula, yet pre-service teachers often report limited preparation for translating CT concepts into instructional practice. This systematic literature review examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) supports pre-service teachers’ instructional design and what the available evidence implies for CT-oriented teaching. Using the PRISMA approach, the review synthesised 26 empirical studies identified through Scopus and ScienceDirect under the original eligibility criteria. The evidence base was heterogeneous: only two studies were coded as explicitly addressing CT integration, fifteen as implicitly CT-aligned, and nine as having no identifiable CT integration. Accordingly, indirect studies are treated as contextual evidence rather than direct evidence of CT instructional design. Across the literature, GenAI was used for ideation, lesson planning, feedback, multimedia generation, and iterative refinement. Several studies reported gains or positive experiences in efficiency, confidence, engagement, creativity, or instructional design competence; however, these outcomes were study-specific and should not be generalised as improvements in CT competence. Several studies have linked more productive use of GenAI to human evaluation, AI literacy, pedagogical or subject-matter knowledge, and structured frameworks or training. Reported risks included inaccurate or inconsistent outputs, hallucinations, overreliance, metacognitive laziness, and ethical concerns. Because the search was limited to Scopus and ScienceDirect and applied an open-access criterion, the review may be affected by database and accessibility bias. Overall, direct evidence that GenAI improves CT-specific instructional design remains preliminary; the broader literature more strongly supports a conditional role for GenAI as a pedagogical scaffold in CT-relevant instructional design.

items.title: Advanced Product and Systems Design Engineering in the Era of Autonomous Robotics and the Internet of Robotic Things (IoRT)
items.abstract: The rapid convergence of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), distributed sensor networks, and edge-native artificial intelligence has transformed modern technology from isolated mechanical devices into complex, interconnected ecosystems. At the heart of this transformation lies Product and Systems Design Engineering (PSDE), a multidisciplinary discipline that bridges mechatronic engineering, human-centered design, software architecture, and systems engineering. This paper presents an extended theoretical and methodological framework for PSDE tailored specifically to Autonomous Robotics and the Internet of Things (IoT)—collectively conceptualized as the Internet of Robotic Things (IoRT).We systematically examine the multi-layered lifecycle of IoRT development, addressing critical trade-offs between dynamic mechanical optimization, deterministic edge-computing, wireless network latency, cyber-physical security, and human-robot interaction (HRI). Furthermore, we detail the implementation of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation paradigms as mechanisms for risk mitigation and cost reduction. The paper concludes by outlining future design directions under the Industry 5.0 paradigm, highlighting the role of generative design, bio-inspired robotics, and circular lifecycle economics.

items.title: AI Agent-Driven Datacenter Optimizer: A Guardrailed, Explainable LLM Orchestrator for Cloud Platform Management
items.abstract: Modern datacenters must balance three objectives that often conflict: keeping hardware within safe thermal limits, meeting latency expectations for high-priority work, and reducing the cost and carbon footprint of electricity. Traditional controllers handle these with fixed rules or heavily engineered optimization pipelines. This paper presents Grid Control, an autonomous datacenter orchestration system in which a large language model (LLM) acts as the decision-making agent. A simulated multi-region datacenter (5 regions, 15 servers, 60 chipsets) streams telemetry every second. Every decision interval the agent receives a frozen telemetry window and selects exactly one action from a small, closed vocabulary: shift_within_server, shift_within_region, migrate_region, or pass. A prioritized policy ranks overheating first, latency and load balance second, and cost and carbon third. Safety is enforced outside the model by a guardrail layer that routes high-criticality or administratorprohibited actions to a human approval queue. A feedback loop returns measured outcomes of past actions to the prompt as incontext learning signal, and a scope-restricted explainability module answers operator questions about the agent's behavior. Over 20 paired simulation runs, a deterministic stand-in for the agent's policy reduced time spent above the 68 °C threshold by about 24% and carbon-weighted load by about 9% relative to a no-agent baseline, with about 3% lower electricity cost. LLM-inthe-loop evaluation is left to future work. The contribution is an architecture and a reproducible testbed for studying safe, explainable, LLM-driven infrastructure control.

items.title: AI and Data Protection
items.abstract: Abstract This chapter examines how artificial intelligence transforms personal data processing and creates compliance challenges for organizations using predictive, generative, and agentic systems. It outlines the UK GDPR, the Data Protection Act 2018, the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, regulatory guidance, and the EU AI Act. The chapter analyses lawful bases, automated decision-making, training data acquisition, transparency, explainability, data subject rights, workplace monitoring, and governance responsibilities associated with AI deployment. It also addresses synthetic media, harmful content, cybersecurity risks, international transfers, procurement obligations, risk mitigation measures, and accountability standards for autonomous systems in public and private sector contexts. Finally, the chapter emphasizes practical compliance through impact assessments, privacy notices, vendor oversight, technical safeguards, organizational controls, and structured AI governance frameworks.

items.title: AI Factchecking in the Bulgarian Language – Mission (Im)Possible?
items.abstract: Abstract: Factchecking is among the key mechanisms for addressing information disorder. In the context of the growing integration of artificial intelligence, particularly large language models, into the information environment, the need for reliable information is increasing while access to it is more challenging. Thus, generative artificial intelligence can be both – an asset and a risk to factcheckers. The present study aims to examine the extent to which Claude.ai and ChatGPT can factcheck claims in Bulgarian. The experiment was conducted using a free skill developed by Nauka.bg. The claims were selected from the “Verified” section of Factcheck.bg, the largest fact-checking platform in Bulgaria. Through comparative content analysis, the study found that in most cases both models correctly identify false claims in accordance with Factcheck.bg’s publications. Claude.ai demonstrates a more authoritative tone and provides concise explanations supporting its verdicts. ChatGPT is more hesitant but offers greater detail, precision, and clarity in its explanations. Notably, ChatGPT rarely references its sources, whereas Claude.ai occasionally links to unreliable sources. A positive trend is Claude.ai’s note to consult official factchecking organizations and verified information sources.The results confirm the hypothesis that artificial intelligence can assist factcheckers but cannot replace human expertise in the verification process. Keywords: disinformation, factchecking, artificial intelligence, large language models, ChatGPT, Claude.ai.

items.title: AI literacy is directly associated with positive attitudes and indirectly associated with negative attitudes through AI anxiety: a cross-sectional study of preservice teachers
items.abstract: Introduction Positive and negative attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI) may have partly distinct psychological correlates. This cross-sectional study examined whether AI anxiety statistically accounted for associations between AI literacy and positive and negative attitudes toward AI among preservice teachers. Methods Participants were 335 preservice teachers enrolled in a faculty of education in Türkiye. Data were collected using the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale, and a personal information form. Two indirect-effect models were estimated using PROCESS Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, controlling for prior AI training. Results AI literacy was negatively associated with AI anxiety and positively associated with positive attitudes toward AI. AI anxiety was positively associated with negative attitudes but was not significantly associated with positive attitudes. The indirect association through AI anxiety was significant for negative attitudes but not for positive attitudes, and a direct bootstrap contrast confirmed that the two indirect effects differed significantly (B = −0.118, 95% CI [−0.201, −0.039]). Prior AI training was not significantly associated with either attitude dimension. A sensitivity analysis excluding the three reverse-worded AI literacy items reproduced this pattern. Discussion The findings indicate that positive and negative attitudes toward AI may have partly distinct psychological correlates: AI literacy is directly related to positive evaluations, whereas its association with negative evaluations is statistically linked to AI anxiety. Because the data are cross-sectional, the indirect effects should not be interpreted as evidence of causal mediation.

items.title: AI Service Investment and Information Disclosure Under Financing Strategies in a Tourism Live-Streaming Supply Chain: The Roles of Government Regulation and Platform Altruism
items.abstract: Live-streaming plays a vital role in tourism product marketing. Consumers often struggle to obtain sufficient product information through live-streaming, leading to information asymmetry and low trust, which hinder transaction efficiency. To address these challenges, an increasing number of live-streaming platforms are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) services to help consumers better understand tourism products. However, investment in AI services requires substantial financial resources, while suppliers’ information disclosure directly affects the transparency of tourism product information. A Stackelberg game model examines how government regulation and financing strategies shape supplier information disclosure, platform AI investment, and supply chain profits. The results show the following: (1) The platform’s financing choice is not determined solely by financing costs. The relative advantage of supplier financing over bank financing depends jointly on relative financing rates, consumers’ sensitivity to AI services, and the platform’s altruistic preference; (2) Neither strategy dominates. Subsidies are more advantageous when reward-and-penalty intensity is low, whereas reward-and-penalty regulation becomes preferable as the intensity increases. (3) Platform altruism boosts AI investment and supplier profit but may reduce platform profit when commissions are low or consumers are less AI-sensitive. These findings provide theoretical guidance for live-streaming platforms to optimize their financing and AI service investment decisions, and for governments to design differentiated information disclosure regulations.

items.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive review of the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital twin (DT) technologies in advanced predictive maintenance (PdM) in modern industrial ecosystems. Traditional maintenance strategies (from reactive maintenance to planned preventive maintenance) often do not account for random degradation patterns, resulting in unplanned equipment downtime or unnecessary operating expenses. By combining real-time Internet of Things (IoT) multi-sensor telemetry streams with high-fidelity physical information and data-driven virtual replicas, AI-powered digital twins provide continuous health monitoring, immediate anomaly isolation and accurate Remaining Useful Life (RUL) calculation. This paper systematically reviews key architectural frameworks, machine learning and deep learning paradigms, edge-cloud deployment topologies, prominent industrial challenges, and future research avenues in Industry 4.0.

items.title: AI-Based Plagiarism Checker: A Review of Text Similarity, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and AI-Obfuscated Plagiarism Detection
items.abstract: Digital documents, paraphrasing tools and large language models have made plagiarism much harder to catch than plain copy-and-paste matching. This review looks at five research papers that approach academic plagiarism detection from different directions: a systematic literature survey, text-based feature selection, deep learning, a comparison of detection techniques, and the detection of AI-obfuscated plagiarism in modeling assignments. Between them, the studies draw on lexical overlap, sentence structure, semantic similarity, writing style and token sequences taken from structured modeling artifacts. One study pairs Chi-square feature selection with a Support Vector Machine (SVM) and reports F-measure scores of 89.34% on PAN 2013 and 92.95% on PAN 2014; another reports that its LSTM-based system placed first among the systems it was compared with on the same benchmarks. A more recent approach for modeling assignments normalizes tokens, matches them automatically and leaves the final judgement to a human inspector, which makes it more resistant to AI-based obfuscation. Taken together, the papers show that no single similarity measure can handle every kind of plagiarism. A practical AI-based checker should therefore combine fast candidate retrieval, several text and structure features, carefully validated machine-learning models and human review. Open problems include resistance to paraphrasing, coverage of datasets and languages, fair evaluation, and the danger of reading a detector score as conclusive proof.

items.title: AI-Based Smart Cow Shelter Analysis and Management System Using Internet of Things and Machine Learning
items.abstract: Cow shelters need coordination between animal identification, health observations, activity tracking, environmental factors, feed and water supplies, vaccination schedules, medical records, and operational actions. Precision livestock farming has created useful tools using sensors, identification systems and artificial intelligence. Recent reviews still show problems with combining information, checking data quality, making systems work together, and supporting decisions [1] [2] [7] [10] [24]. This paper introduces a cow-shelter system that connects RFID animal tagging, different types of IoT sensors, ESP32-based data collection at the edge, Wi-Fi communication, Flask web services, MySQL databases, clear rule-based alerts, and machine learning—all within a single management process. The system links animal data with shelter-zone details and keeps track of time, data quality, management actions, and past alerts. The analysis is done in stages: simple rules give alerts, and machine learning comes later once enough labelled and checked data is available. Features used in the analysis include sensor readings, changes over time, average trends, activity summaries, environmental data, and feed and water status. A repeatable way to test the system is created, measuring sensing delay, alert timing, data transmission reliability, dashboard speed, recovery after failure, and how well predictions work. The main contribution is not in technology but in the full system design: an information-to-action process built around animal identity, multiple sensors, resource tracking, records, analysis, alerts, and human input. The paper does not give accuracy or timing results and does not claim the individual parts are new.

items.title: AI-Driven Digital Twin Framework for Sustainable Fisheries Management and Intelligent Aquatic Water Resource Monitoring
items.abstract: Digital twins are increasingly proposed as a means of linking aquatic observations, predictive models and management decisions. Their relevance to sustainability nevertheless depends on more than the speed or accuracy of an artificial intelligence model. This critical narrative review examines the evidence connecting digital-twin architectures with capture fisheries, aquaculture and freshwater and coastal water-quality monitoring. Literature published through 30 July 2026 was selected through targeted scholarly searches, citation tracing and bibliographic verification, with particular attention to observation quality, independent validation, operational feedback and management outcomes. The synthesis distinguishes a digital model, a continuously updated digital representation and a decision-linked twin, and separates component performance from demonstrated ecological benefit. Evidence supports advances in image-based monitoring, satellite retrievals, hybrid environmental prediction and selected field deployments. It is substantially less conclusive regarding sustained stock recovery, equitable allocation or ecosystem-scale benefits attributable to a complete digital-twin system. Important limitations include imperfect observability, inappropriate spatial and temporal validation, uncertain transfer between environments, simulator-dependent policy optimisation and incomplete treatment of human behaviour. Apparent disagreement between promising technical demonstrations and limited management evidence largely reflects different endpoints and system boundaries rather than a simple conflict over technological feasibility. A federated, decision-centred framework is proposed in which traceable observations support uncertainty-aware state estimation, explicit management objectives, constrained decision support and independently audited outcomes. The framework includes staged deployment, human authorisation, local data governance and lifecycle assessment; it is an unvalidated synthesis rather than an implemented system. Near-term priorities are prospective forecasting benchmarks, comparative management trials, failure-tolerant monitoring and participatory evaluation in data-limited fisheries. Digital twins are most defensible as accountable extensions of existing environmental observation and adaptive management, not as substitutes for ecological understanding, enforceable institutions or legitimate collective decisions.

items.title: AI-Driven Project Management Automation: A Framework for Task Prioritization, Progress Monitoring, and Risk Identification
items.abstract: Project management requires coordination of tasks, deadlines, dependencies, resources, and risks. Manual status reporting and inconsistent prioritisation can make emerging delivery problems difficult to identify. This paper proposes and demonstrates a framework connecting task prioritisation, progress monitoring, and task-delay risk identification. The framework combines transparent rule-based scoring, monitoring flags, a machine-learning classifier, and human review. A prototype was evaluated using 1,000 generated task records, with a Decision Tree compared against a majority-class baseline on a held-out test set. The Decision Tree achieved 61.0% accuracy, 27.4% precision, 57.5% recall, and an F1-score of 37.1% for the delay class. The baseline achieved 80.0% accuracy but detected no delayed tasks, demonstrating why accuracy alone can be misleading in imbalanced classification. These results describe the prototype experiment and do not establish effectiveness on real project records. The paper concludes that an integrated framework can provide a reproducible basis for further evaluation, with real-world validation required before operational use. Keywords: artificial intelligence, project management automation, task prioritisation, progress monitoring, risk identification, delay prediction, Decision Tree, business analytics

items.title: AI-Enabled Decision Support for Volunteer Allocation in Disaster Management: A Three-Stage Optimization Framework
items.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming disaster management through intelligent decision support, predictive resource allocation, and adaptive operational planning. Volunteer management — a critical yet underexplored challenge in humanitarian logistics — represents a domain where AI-driven optimization can deliver substantial operational gains. This chapter presents a three-stage AI-enabled decision support framework for volunteer allocation in large-scale disaster response. At its core is a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that constitutes the optimization layer of a broader AI-assisted humanitarian logistics ecosystem. The model assigns volunteers to disaster management centers while maximizing demand satisfaction, respecting capacity and travel-time constraints, incorporating individual preferences, enforcing group cohesion to improve long-term retention, and preventing scheduling conflicts. Computational experiments using a synthetic scenario with 100 volunteers, six volunteer types, four disaster management centers, and a seven-day response horizon confirm the model’s feasibility: the MILP solver reaches a solution in under 8 seconds and generates schedules that substantially reduce unmet demand. Sensitivity analysis on the preference–demand trade-off reveals important operational dynamics. The chapter concludes with a roadmap for extending the framework with machine learning demand forecasting, reinforcement learning-based dynamic reassignment, digital twin simulation, and predictive retention modeling — positioning the system as a foundation for next-generation AI tools in disaster humanitarian logistics.

items.title: Airway image analysis systems: a review of datasets, evaluation methodologies, and deep learning approaches
items.abstract: Airway image analysis systems play an increasingly important role in computer-assisted diagnosis, quantitative airway assessment, intervention planning, and respiratory disease management. However, the development of robust airway analysis methods remains challenging due to the complex geometry of airway structures, strong class imbalance, variability in imaging protocols, and the need to preserve anatomical connectivity across multiple spatial scales. Recent advances in topology-aware learning, transformer-based architectures, and foundation-model adaptation have substantially changed the landscape of airway image analysis, motivating an updated review focused specifically on airway-oriented systems. In this narrative review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the datasets, evaluation methodologies, and computational approaches that underpin modern airway image analysis systems. We discuss the imaging modalities and publicly available datasets commonly used for airway analysis and examine their strengths, limitations, and implications for algorithm development and benchmarking. Particular attention is given to evaluation methodologies, including overlap-based, surface-distance, and topology-aware metrics that assess both segmentation accuracy and structural correctness. We further review the evolution of computational approaches, covering convolutional neural networks, transformer-based architectures, hybrid methods, topology-aware and tubular-aware networks, foundation-model adaptations, and data-efficient learning strategies. Finally, we discuss current challenges related to dataset availability, annotation quality, model generalization, topology preservation, and clinical deployment, and outline future research directions toward robust, interpretable, and clinically deployable airway image analysis systems.

items.title: Algebraic Structures for Explainable Artificial Intelligence and Decision-Making Systems
items.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has become an important research direction because intelligent systems are increasingly used to support decisions in complex and uncertain environments. However, the interpretability of a decision depends not only on the final prediction but also on the mathematical structure through which the prediction is obtained. This paper develops an algebraic framework for interpretable multi-criteria decision-making based on bounded ordered structures, weighted aggregation, and explicit criterion-level contributions. A finite set of alternatives is evaluated using normalized criteria, and a weighted score is assigned to each alternative. The framework represents criterion values in a bounded lattice and uses an order-preserving aggregation operator to obtain transparent rankings. Mathematical properties concerning monotonicity, boundedness, score decomposition, and stability under perturbations are established. An illustrative numerical example involving the selection of an artificial intelligence model demonstrates how the framework generates rankings and human-readable explanations. The approach provides a mathematically explicit foundation for decision support and can be extended to fuzzy, linguistic, and neutrosophic environments. The proposed framework and numerical example are illustrative; novelty and performance claims require literature verification and empirical validation. Keywords: Abstract algebra; lattice theory; explainable artificial intelligence; multi-criteria decision-making; interpretable decision systems; weighted aggregation.

items.title: Algorithmic Childhood Future-AI Prediction Systems and the Pre-Emption of Choice in Young Consumers
items.abstract: The fast adoption of Artificial Intelligence in the child-facing digital ecosystem has changed marketing into a reactive personalization model to a predictive and pre-emptive model of shaping choice. This chapter envisions an algorithmic childhood futures, in which AI technologies predict preferences and restructure the choice environment of children prior to the desire developing consciously. Based on the interdisciplinary theory and the latest case studies provided in the educational platforms and smart toy ecosystems, the chapter proves how predictive architectures may promote engagement and gradually reduce exploration and redistribute agency. This analysis puts the concept of algorithmic influence in a new perspective, as temporal harm, with its long-term developmental consequences, that are still poorly dealt with in existing governance models. To create a balance between innovation, commercial goals and digital well-being, the chapter ends with the suggestions to child-centered design and managerial principles.

items.title: An investigation of lifestyle behaviors, mental well-being, and work-related outcomes among female teachers: mixed-methods evidence for occupational health promotion
items.abstract: Background Teachers’ health and quality of life are important to school health and education policy. This study examined lifestyle behaviors, mental well-being, satisfaction, and health-related absence among female schoolteachers in Saudi Arabia. Methods A mixed-methods study in the Eastern Province combined a cross-sectional questionnaire completed by 562 female government-school teachers with semi-structured interviews with 19 teachers. Mental well-being was assessed using the WHO-5. Associations were examined using Spearman correlation and multivariable logistic regression. Interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis with an inductive approach. Results Poor mental well-being (WHO-5 ≤ 50) was reported by 58.4% of teachers, and 24.4% scored ≤28. No moderate-intensity activity was reported by 42.3%; 77.4% of 561 respondents slept six hours or less. Unhealthy foods were consumed several times per week or almost daily by 52.5%; only 29.9% consumed fruit and vegetables daily. Poor or very poor sleep quality was reported by 19.4%, and tobacco use by 3.4%. Overall, 27.9% brushed their teeth less than twice daily, and 52.1% last visited a dentist over two years earlier. Tooth or gum pain at least sometimes during the preceding three months was reported by 61.9%. Sleep quality and duration showed moderate positive correlations with well-being ( r = 0.390 and 0.302, respectively; p < 0.001). Physical activity, dietary behaviors, toothbrushing, and oral pain were also associated with well-being. Higher teaching load was weakly associated with lower satisfaction ( r = −0.098, p = 0.020). Lifestyle and satisfaction scores remained associated with good well-being after adjustment (OR = 1.051, 95% CI: 1.030–1.073; and 1.035, 95% CI: 1.022–1.048, respectively). Self-rated health also remained associated with good well-being. Lower lifestyle and well-being scores were associated with more health-related absence (all p < 0.05). Five themes described demanding workdays, barriers to healthy routines, emotional strain, work extending into home life, and occupational health concerns. Conclusion Unhealthy daily routines and poor mental well-being were common among teachers. These findings support greater attention to teacher health in education policy. School health promotion should include manageable work demands, time for rest, and access to preventive care. Sustained investment in workplace health promotion may support teachers’ well-being and quality of life.

items.title: An Old Answer to a New Problem: The Degree-Free Model for Higher Education in the Age of AI
items.abstract: Generative AI has not created the governance crisis in higher education credentialing; it has made it harder to ignore. The academic degree is higher education’s principal instrument for governing access to occupations. Its signaling value depends on assessed work reflecting individual competence. AI weakens that link: in blind marking, AI-written exam answers went largely undetected and, on average, outscored students, while detection tools trail each new model. Strengthening surveillance restores procedural control only at the cost of assessment validity. Drawing on credentialism and signaling theory, this paper argues that the response may need to include institutional redesign, not only pedagogical adjustment. It proposes a degree-free model, illustrated by the yeshiva: a centuries-old institution organized around formation, community, and recognized mastery rather than certification. Labor markets already partly follow this logic, as employers substitute direct observation of performance for the degree within three to five years of hire. Three recommendations follow. Outside safety-critical fields, institutions could stop issuing degrees while continuing to teach. Public investment should shift from surveillance-based assessment toward authentic evaluation. Reform should be differentiated by field, retaining mandatory credentialing in licensed and safety-critical professions. The model is offered as a proposition for debate, not a blueprint.

items.title: Apex Horizon: A Dual-Theater Edge-Cloud Telemetry and Multimodal Nowcasting Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction and Agro-Forestry Resilience
items.abstract: This technical pre-print presents the operational architecture and experimental methodology of Apex Horizon, a mission-critical cyber-physical geospatial telemetry platform designed for real-time natural hazard nowcasting, environmental monitoring, and microclimate risk mitigation under degraded communication infrastructure. The system establishes an auditable multi-stream data architecture integrating open earth-observation feeds: geostationary satellite clean infrared radiometry (NOAA GOES-16 ABI and JMA Himawari-9 AHI), shortwave infrared differential fog detection (ΔTfog), synoptic aviation METAR observations, multi-source anemometer arrays, and seismic feeds. To evaluate operational robustness across distinct climatic regimes, the platform employs a dual-theater operational testbed spanning subtropical continental basins and temperate archipelago zones. Furthermore, the architecture integrates a reproducible three-tier data persistence model (relational, geospatial via PostGIS, and high-dimensional vector similarity indexing via pgvector with HNSW) to decouple raw sensor streams, upstream service trust metrics, and edge heuristic baselines. Experimental evaluation demonstrates complete telemetry preservation through an offline-first synchronization engine and resilient localized situational awareness during central backhaul outages.

items.title: Argument-First Versus Language-First Generative AI Feedback in Chinese EFL Argumentative Writing: A Randomized Study
items.abstract: This eight-week randomized study examined how the order of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) feedback shaped revision and near-term independent writing among 132 Chinese English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) undergraduates. Students received argument-first (AF; n = 67) or language-first (LF; n = 65) feedback; 64 pairs underwent within-class, within-pair randomization, and four unmatched students were randomized within class. Both modules were independently generated from each initial draft (D0) and locked before release. Students completed two revisions (D1 and D2) across three tasks and a new-topic, AI-free transfer task. Adjusted AF–LF differences in D0–D2 change favored AF for overall quality (0.811 points, 95% CI [0.424, 1.198]) and argumentation (1.102 points, 95% CI [0.668, 1.536]), but not language quality (0.020 points, 95% CI [−0.381, 0.420]). Revision depth and implementation showed stage-specific crossovers. Language contrasts did not survive primary Holm adjustment, although complete-pair sensitivity analysis detected a crossover. Argumentation transfer favored AF (1.057 points, 95% CI [0.508, 1.606]); overall transfer was less consistent, with the complete-pair interval including zero (0.685 points, 95% CI [−0.111, 1.481]). Module type was structurally linked to release stage, so stage-specific contrasts describe sequence-by-stage configurations rather than isolated content or order effects. The findings support cautious use of staged feedback when argumentative development is the instructional priority.

items.title: ARIFICIAL INTELLEGENCE AND ENGLISH READING MOTIVATION INFLUENCING COMMUNICATION SKILLS AMONG PAKISTANI UNDERGRADUATE COLLEGE STUDENTS
items.abstract: The fast incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has changed how university students’ access, evaluate, produce, and communicate scientific information. At the same time, English reading motivation remains significant for Pakistani college undergraduate students because English is extensively used in academic, educational, lingua franca and scientific contexts. English language is also enjoying prestigious status in Pakistan. This study examines AI literacy and English reading motivation as predictors of science communication skills among Pakistani students. AI literacy is theorized as students’ ability to understand, use, evaluate, and ethically engage with AI technologies, while English reading motivation refers to students’ interest in reading for educational, academic and other purposes. Science communication skills include the skill to explain scientific concepts accurately, clearly, ethically, and appropriately to in this context with multi socio-economic and culture backgrounds of Pakistan. Existing literature suggests that AI literacy involves more than technological usage and includes critical evaluation and ethical awareness. Likewise, research on English-medium instruction indicates that language competence can influence students’ participation and learning experiences. This study has used a quantitative, correlational-predictive design involving collegiate students from Pakistani higher education institutions. Data have been collected from N=250 college students through standardized questionnaires and a science communication performance task. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, and multiple regression analysis have been completed. The study shows that there are evidences for assimilating AI literacy, English proficiency, and science communication into college programs.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the 2027 Elections: Comparing Urban and Rural Voters' Responses to AI-Generated Campaign Messages in Abia State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering Nigerian electoral communication ahead of the 2027 general elections, raising concerns about authenticity, trust and misinformation. This exploratory study examined how voters aged 18–40 in Abia State, Nigeria, understand, feel about and respond to AI-generated and AI-assisted campaign messages, and how urban/semi-urban and rural voters compare. Method: A qualitative exploratory design was adopted. Twenty voters (ten urban/semi-urban and ten rural) were purposively selected from communities across Abia State and interviewed individually using six AI-generated or AI-assisted campaign materials (CM1–CM6), supplemented by observation notes. Data were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and interpreted with the Elaboration Likelihood Model. Findings: AI familiarity varied within both groups rather than simply between them. Participants separated emotional appeal from credibility, and realistic fabrication caused more concern than obvious satire. The messages stimulated attention, discussion and verification more readily than candidate support, and rural participants relied more on interpersonal and community verification networks. Conclusion: Within this sample, AI-generated campaign messages shaped electoral judgement through credibility, emotional appeal, realism and verification conditions rather than automatic vote conversion. As exploratory findings, these are not statistically generalisable but offer propositions for larger studies.

items.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety and nurses’ turnover intention during healthcare digital transformation: the mediating role of occupational fatigue
items.abstract: Background The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare is associated with new psychological challenges. However, the extent of its impact on nursing workforce stability is unclear. Aim To explore the relationship between AI anxiety and turnover intention of clinical nurses, and the mediating effect of occupational fatigue and the moderating effect of emotional intelligence (EI). Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted from March to June 2026 among 404 clinical nurses from four hospitals in Jiangsu Province, China. Data were collected using the AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS), Health Workers’ Occupational Fatigue Scale (HWOFS), Turnover Intention Scale (TIS) and Wong and Law Emotional Intelligence Scale (WLEIS). Mediation was tested using structural equation modelling with bootstrap resampling, while moderation was tested using moderated regression analysis. Results Differences in baseline turnover intentions across age, department, and professional title level were statistically significant (all p < 0.001). Path analysis showed that AI anxiety was positively associated with occupational fatigue (β = 0.611, p < 0.001) and turnover intention (β = 0.530, p < 0.001). Occupational fatigue partially mediated the association between AI anxiety and turnover intention (indirect effect = 0.299, 95% CI: 0.129, 0.379). EI had a significant negative main effect on occupational fatigue (b = −0.257, p < 0.001), but it did not significantly moderate the association between AI anxiety and occupational fatigue. Conclusion AI anxiety is significantly correlated with the turnover intention of clinical nurses, and occupational fatigue may represent a potential pathway linking AI anxiety and turnover intention. Although EI is associated with lower levels of occupational fatigue, it fails to cushion the impact of AI anxiety, a specific stressor. Hospital administrators should focus on targeted AI literacy improvement plans and specific fatigue relief strategies to retain clinical nursing staff.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Health in the Diagnosis of Leprosy: Current Advances and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Leprosy remains a significant public health challenge in endemic regions, where delayed diagnosis leads to irreversible nerve damage, disability, and ongoing transmission. To address the need for innovative diagnostic strategies, artificial intelligence (AI) and digital health technologies have emerged as promising tools. This review explores the current applications of machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and mobile health platforms in leprosy diagnosis and management. AI-based image analysis demonstrates strong potential for identifying characteristic skin lesions and differentiating leprosy from other dermatological conditions. Additionally, predictive algorithms and smartphone-based telemedicine expand access to specialized care in underserved settings while facilitating contact tracing, surveillance, and treatment monitoring. Despite these encouraging advances, significant challenges remain, including limited high-quality annotated datasets, algorithmic bias, a lack of external validation, and data privacy concerns. Ultimately, AI-driven digital health solutions should complement rather than replace clinical expertise. Prioritizing multicenter collaborations, explainable AI models, and secure data integration will be essential to strengthen global leprosy control programs, improve patient outcomes, and reduce the burden of this neglected tropical disease.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND VOCAL BIOMARKERS IN ASTHMA DIAGNOSIS AND MONITORING: A NARRATIVE REVIEW
items.abstract: Considering that chronic respiratory diseases, such as asthma, represent a global challenge, their continuous monitoring is often limited by the need for specialized equipment. Artificial Intelligence (AI) applied to the acoustic analysis of cough and voice emerges as a non-invasive alternative. It aims to investigate how vocal biomarkers can be isolated for the specific detection and monitoring of asthma. To this end, we proceed to a narrative review that synthesizes recent literature on the application of machine learning algorithms. In this way, it is observed that changes in respiratory mechanics modify extractable acoustic parameters, such as MFCCs. Several architectures demonstrate high accuracy, frequently exceeding 85% to 90% by fusing spectral and temporal features. Data augmentation tools overcome sample scarcity, and advanced filters mitigate ambient noise on smartphones. This allows us to conclude that AI-processed vocal biomarkers hold significant clinical potential for outpatient screening. The standardization of recording protocols and validation in multicenter cohorts are essential for the safe integration of this technology into telemedicine.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for facial soft‐tissue landmark localization, measurement, and classification in orthodontics: A systematic review
items.abstract: Abstract This systematic review provides a broad overview of three distinct applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in facial soft‐tissue assessment: landmark localization, automated facial measurement, and classification of soft‐tissue conditions in orthodontic and dentofacial evaluation. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, ClinicalTrials.gov, Google Scholar, and Open Science Framework were searched. Studies using 2D facial photographs, 3D facial scans, or AI‐generated facial models were included. Risk of bias was assessed with an adapted QUADAS‐2 tool and certainty of evidence with GRADE. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261452521). Fifteen studies were included. Landmark‐localization performance varied substantially by imaging modality, landmark definition, data set, reference standard, and error metric; central and anatomically well‐defined landmarks were generally more accurate than peripheral or subjective points. Agreement for AI‐derived measurements ranged from poor to excellent, with ICCs of approximately 0.01–0.984. Classification accuracy ranged from approximately 0.83 to 0.98, with AUCs up to 0.98. Given only two narrowly scoped classification studies, these findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis‐generating rather than broadly generalizable. Because of substantial methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized qualitatively. Current evidence supports AI as an adjunctive tool, but routine clinical implementation requires robust external validation and clinician oversight. PROSPERO registration: CRD420261452521

items.title: Artificial intelligence for vascular minimally invasive surgery: techniques, clinical integration, and challenges
items.abstract: Introduction Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. Methods A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Results Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. Discussion AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Middle and Secondary Education: Instructional Opportunities, Limitations and Ethical Considerations
items.abstract: Middle and secondary school educators should utilize and implement Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a support tool for instruction, not a replacement for their pedagogy and lesson planning. Utilizing and implementing AI can assist with lesson planning, differentiation, feedback, and generating learning materials; and its uses should be guided by clear expectations, professional judgment, and school policy. Educators should also teach their students how to use AI ethically, verify outputs for accuracy and bias, and protect student privacy by avoiding sensitive data. Most importantly, assessments should be designed to show genuine student understanding, with AI used transparently and appropriately. The best available published advice concurs that the usage of AI within an educator’s pedagogy significantly enhances middle and secondary school students’ learning. This article offers practical guidance for educators who use or plan to use AI in the classroom, while also highlighting policy recommendations to support effective educational practices.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in religious education: teacher perspectives from a national professional development context
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines teachers’ perceptions of and orientations to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the context of Religious Education (RE), drawing on survey data collected from 54 in-service RE teachers participating in the SUB8 professional development programme in Greece. Using a descriptive survey design grounded in the frameworks of Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), AI literacy, and digital self-efficacy, the study maps teachers’ reported practices, competencies, and concerns across seven thematic dimensions. Findings indicate generally positive orientations towards AI-assisted instructional design within this cohort, alongside significant theological and pedagogical concerns regarding its use in spiritually sensitive contexts. Qualitative responses point to three recurring themes: the productive utility of AI for lesson preparation and differentiation; persistent concerns about accuracy, depth, and the reliability of AI-generated content; and a strong consensus that AI must function as a supplementary pedagogical tool, subordinate to the relational and experiential dimensions of RE. Because participants were self-selected members of an AI-focused training programme and were surveyed immediately upon its completion, these findings are interpreted as descriptive of this specific professional development context rather than of Greek RE teachers in general. The study complements recent comparative evidence from Germany and Poland by providing, to the author’s knowledge, the first empirical account of AI perceptions among RE teachers within an Orthodox national professional development context, and it foregrounds a theological and epistemological dimension still largely absent from AI-in-education research.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Integration and Its Effectiveness on Higher Vocational Education Management and School–Enterprise Talent Training
items.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) integration, management effectiveness, and school–enterprise collaborative talent training at Guangzhou Huali Vocational College of Science and Technology, China. A descriptive-correlational quantitative design involved 159 students and 101 teachers during the second semester of academic year 2025–2026. Students were included through total enumeration and teachers through purposive sampling. A researcher-developed questionnaire was validated by five experts and pilot-tested with 30 individuals; Cronbach’s alpha was 0.96. Analysis used frequencies, percentages, weighted means, t tests, one-way analysis of variance, and Pearson correlations. Both groups rated AI integration as high, management effectiveness to a high extent, and training success to a high degree. Students’ assessments differed significantly by enterprise exposure across all three constructs; teachers’ AI integration assessments differed by position. AI integration correlated positively with management effectiveness for students (r = 0.8839) and teachers (r = 0.9225). Management effectiveness correlated positively with training success for students (r = 0.9399) and teachers (r = 0.9586). The findings support coordinated curriculum, assessment, supervision, faculty development, and workplace learning. A Comprehensive AI Integration Framework was proposed to strengthen institutional practices and collaborative training. The relationships indicate association rather than causation.

items.title: Artificial intelligence literacy and innovative behavior among clinical nurses: the roles of AI self-efficacy and organizational innovation climate
items.abstract: Objective To investigate the current status and related factors of innovative behavior among clinical nurses in tertiary hospitals and explore the relationships and pathways among artificial intelligence literacy, AI self-efficacy, organizational innovation climate, and nurse innovative behavior, for providing a basis for targeted nursing management strategies. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted on 850 nurses from six tertiary medical institutions using a stratified survey approach in Yueyang city, Hunan province, from June to July 2026, in the General Information Questionnaire, Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale, Organizational Innovation Climate Scale, and Nurse Innovative Behavior Scale were used. AMOS 24.0 was used to conduct confirmatory factor analysis to assess the model fit of the scales. SPSS 26.0 was used for descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, Pearson correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression. PROCESS macro version 4.2 Models 4 and 14 tested mediation and moderated mediation effects. Results A total of 850 valid questionnaires were obtained, with a valid questionnaire rate of 95.3%. The mean nurse innovative behavior score was 37.93±6.50. The measurement model for the four scales showed good fit, and the scales demonstrated good convergent validity and some evidence of discriminant validity. Artificial intelligence literacy, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, organizational innovation climate, and innovative behavior showed positive associations with one another (r = 0.609–0.797, P < 0.01). Educational level, professional title, participation in research or innovation activities, artificial intelligence literacy, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, and organizational innovation climate were factors associated with nurse innovative behavior and explained 60.9% of the total variance. Artificial intelligence self-efficacy partially mediated the relationship between artificial intelligence literacy and nurse innovative behavior. The indirect effect was 0.322, with a 95% CI of 0.243–0.403, accounting for 52.90% of the total effect. Organizational innovation climate moderated the relationship between artificial intelligence self-efficacy and nurse innovative behavior (b = 0.051, P < 0.01). The index of moderated mediation was 0.041, with a 95% CI of 0.009–0.078. Conclusion AI literacy was closely related to nurse innovative behavior, with AI self-efficacy as a partial mediator and organizational innovation climate as a moderator. Nursing management may focus on AI competencies, application confidence, and organizational support.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness in Bangladesh’s Public Administration: Linking Digital Leadership, Employee AI Capability, and Service Innovation
items.abstract: AI will emerge as a significant force behind administrative change, although public organisations vary in their preparedness to do so. This paper investigates the impact of digital leadership and employee AI ability on artificial intelligence preparedness and innovation in services in the Bangladesh public administration. A four-reflective construct survey model was created, including digital leadership, employee AI capability, AI readiness, and service innovation. It was analysed with a synthetic dataset of 835 cases that are intended to test the methodology and prove PLS-SEM. The data were evaluated using descriptive statistics, common method bias tests, evaluation of the measurement model, structural model, mediation, and predictive assessment. The findings revealed that the positive impacts of digital leadership and employee AI capability on AI preparedness were significant. Service innovation was also positively impacted by AI readiness significantly. Digital leadership and employee AI capability had a direct impact on service innovation. Both relationships were partially mediated by AI readiness. The model explained 45.4% of the variance in AI readiness and 41.0% of the variance in service innovation. All the predictive relevance values were positive and the PLS model yielded lower prediction errors than linear benchmark. The results reveal a readiness pathway that is coherent where leadership, employee capability, and institutional preparedness contribute to innovation in the delivery of public services.

items.title: Artificial intelligence use patterns, attitudes, and psychological distress among medical students: a cross-sectional survey
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are widely used by medical students, but associations of general use frequency and AI-related attitudes with psychological distress remain unclear. Methods All 1,275 active students at one Turkish medical faculty were invited to an anonymous online survey conducted from 1 April to 1 May 2026; 249 of 251 respondents consented. Measures included general AI use, an investigator-translated 13-item Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale (ATAI), and the validated Turkish Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21. A general-distress composite was the primary outcome, and hierarchical regression used HC3 robust standard errors. Results AI use was reported by 95.6% of participants, and 50.2% reported daily use. Mean doubled DASS-21 total was 56.97 (SD 31.55). The ATAI three-factor model showed mixed fit (CFI = .898, TLI = .872, RMSEA = .107, SRMR = .070). AI-frequency categories did not improve the adjusted model at the block level (change in R -squared = .016, p = .111; robust global p = .088). Adding exploratory ATAI factors increased R-squared by.052 ( p = .002; robust global p = .009); Benefit was inversely, and Risk and Use positively, associated with distress. Subscale sensitivity analyses preserved coefficient directions, but only the inverse Benefit-Anxiety association survived correction across 15 additional focal tests ( q = .032). Conclusion AI use was nearly universal and served both educational and personal/non-educational purposes, but this sample did not provide stable evidence of an overall association between general use frequency and distress. ATAI associations are exploratory and may reflect measurement or common-method processes. Longitudinal multicenter studies should use formally adapted measures and objective indicators of AI engagement.
